openwritingkit-user-cmonjauregui@gmail.c.title: Til Death Do Us Part
openwritingkit-user-cmonjauregui@gmail.c.description:
It all happened too fast. Their first meeting, the couple of months before it turned into an engagement, the trimester before they tied the knot. It wasn’t perfect, far from it; it was passionate, impulsive, breathtaking, agonisingly beautiful. So when Lucy learnt from a pair of terrifyingly well-dressed men who looked far too much like those guys on MIB that her wife, her newly-wed wife, had passed away on a tragic car accident… Well, let’s say she didn’t take it too well.
Matters turned even worse when, on a vacation over 10 thousand kilometres away from home - one her best friends made her agree on after three years of grieving -, she encountered Taylor, said dead wife, resurged from her supposed grave and seemingly not remembering a single thing about her.

openwritingkit-story-1752901487166-docum.name: Weekend at Taylor’s
openwritingkit-story-1752901487166-docum.content:
Lucy Green is, per her own standards, a very common fellow.

It starts with her name. How could a girl’s name in Britain get more common than Lucy?

(She figures Marys or Chloes or Emilys, or even, God forbid, Sophies could argue with her reasoning. She also figures that is very irrelevant to her point.)

Her last name only makes the matter worse. Green? Being a colour first, category of vegetable second, last name, well, last… it just feels very lacking in creativity. It doesn’t help much that it was popularised by Friends. In lieu of spelling it, she usually has to go with “like the colour” or “just like Rachel Green.” Lacking.

And then again, she has always led a very common life.

She was never first in class, or a big-time athlete, or the school’s most popular girl. She was always pretty, sure, but never striking or breathtaking or any adjective that could sufficiently describe someone you stop in the middle of the street to stare at.

After uni and a very common degree in Accounting (although, she admits, it is an undergraduate course one would usually associate with old people and that was becoming less and less common by the day), she got a very common office job.

Every day she wakes up, takes her warm shower, brushes her teeth, makes breakfast, gets dressed, takes the tube to The City, spends eight hours sitting behind a desk analysing spreadsheets, takes the tube back home, makes dinner, watches a bland romcom on Netflix or one of the hundreds of TV shows she once swore to go through, and goes to sleep.

All this to say, Lucy has always been common, a fact she is, don’t get her wrong, very happy with.

The only uncommon factor in her thirty three years of inhabiting Planet Earth is her wife.

Taylor was never common.

With the only exception of her last name (Scott is, also, a rather popular name, although thankfully not a colour one), Taylor has always been anything but common. She was first in class since kindergarten (a fact Lucy took a lot of joy in hearing from her proud mother-in-law),
